Wairarapa grain storage set to benefit farmers
news.body:
Wairarapa farmers and allied contractors will reap the benefits of a $1.55 million loan from the Regional Infrastructure Fund to support the establishment of a new grain drying and storage facility in Carterton.

The loan will enable farmers to store up to 4000 tonnes of grain in the region instead of trucking it to Manawatu for storage, Associate Regional Development Minister Mark Patterson says.

The creation of the facility will help support more than 300 workers across farming, transport, contracting and advisory services in the region.

“A large locally based facility will improve costs, efficiencies, and resilience for both grain producers and local farmers who rely on the grain for stock feed.

“Growers have had to store excess grain outside the region, which increases costs and reduces margins for both producers and contractors,.

“This has been compounded by rising diesel prices piling on the costs of transporting grain elsewhere for storage and then back again when needed. This investment restores essential infrastructure and keeps more value in Wairarapa.”

A scalable grain-drying and storage facility is more viable and affordable for Wairarapa growers than the storage, seed-cleaning and processing facilities initially proposed, Mr Patterson says.

“Wairarapa farmers will benefit from a new seed-cleaning and processing facility in central Hawke’s Bay that the Government is also supporting with a $3 million RIF loan.”

The funding is subject to the establishment of a grower-led company to build and run the facility, provision of at least $800,000 of grower equity, and suitable site, delivery, consenting and financial arrangements.

news.title: Regional radio strengthened for emergencies
news.body:
The Government is investing in the resilience of independent radio broadcasters to help ensure regional communities can access vital emergency information when electricity, internet or telecommunications services are disrupted.

Regional Development Minister Shane Jones and Emergency Management and Recovery Minister Mark Mitchell today announced a $300,000 grant from the Regional Infrastructure Fund (RIF) to support the Regional Emergency Broadcasting programme.

“Regional radio stations play a vital role in keeping communities informed, particularly when other communication channels fail,” Mr Jones says.

“This RIF investment will strengthen critical communications infrastructure and help ensure New Zealanders can continue to access important information when they need it most.”

The funding will support the installation of back-up generators and associated infrastructure at 10 independently owned regional radio stations throughout the country.

Mr Mitchell says having reliable communication in regional areas is essential during emergencies, and the Regional Emergency Broadcasting programme complements Radio New Zealand’s role as the nationwide emergency radio station network.

“When events disrupt power and telecommunications networks, radio can be one of the most dependable ways for people to receive warnings and updates,” Mr Mitchell says.

“This investment will help communities remain connected to their trusted sources of information during emergencies, supporting response and recovery efforts and improving public safety.”

The work will be co-ordinated by the Independent Media Association in partnership with participating regional broadcasters. The funding will support back-up generation capability, electrical works, fuel storage, site preparation, testing and commissioning. A further $20,000 of co-funding will support project delivery.

Editors’ note

The 10 participating stations are:

Coromandel FM 1XX (Eastern Bay of Plenty) Lake FM (Taupō) Peak FM (Ruapehu District) Central FM (Central Hawke’s Bay) Beach FM 106.3 (Kapiti Coast) Compass FM (North Canterbury) Coast FM (West Coast) South Canterbury 100.3 Radio Central (Central Otago)

news.title: Government backs regional airline Air Napier
news.body:
The Government is continuing its support for regional air services, with Regional Development Minister Shane Jones and Associate Transport Minister James Meager announcing an $845,000 loan to Hawke’s Bay airline Air Napier.

The Regional Infrastructure Fund (RIF) loan will help Air Napier undertake essential upgrades to its fleet and refinance some existing debt.

“Air Napier plays an important role in supporting businesses across Hawke’s Bay and Tairāwhiti, and helping people access essential services,” Mr Jones says.

“For decades, it has provided flights for Hastings-based doctors and nurses travelling to and from Wairoa, saving hours of road travel and helping ensure local communities can access vital healthcare.”

The loan is from the remainder of the Government’s $30 million regional air connectivity package, established in 2025 to support vulnerable regional air services. Air Napier is the final airline to receive support through the package.

“Regional airlines are critical to the economic success of our regions,” Mr Meager says.

“They support tourism, trade and business activity, while also helping maintain essential services during emergencies and civil defence responses.

“During Cyclone Gabrielle, Air Napier helped transport civil defence personnel, medical staff, patients, and urgent supplies, including medicines, up and down the East Coast.”

Mr Meager says regional airlines continue to face significant cost pressures in a challenging operating environment.

“The Government recognises the important role these airlines play in connecting regional communities. That is why we have continued to support the sector, including through the recent announcement of $5.7 million in grants to help meet day-to-day operating costs.”

news.title: Govt nurturing New Zealand’s seed supply chain
news.body:
Hawke’s Bay’s arable sector is set to benefit from a $3 million Regional Infrastructure Fund loan for a new grower-led seed cleaning, processing and storage facility in Central Hawke’s Bay, Associate Regional Development Minister Mark Patterson says.

“Currently, much of the seed grown in Hawke's Bay that requires specialist cleaning and processing is sent outside the region, including to as far away as Canterbury, before it can be sold domestically or exported. This adds cost, creates inefficiencies, and reduces returns for local growers” Mr Patterson says.

Previous government investment in 2023 supported development of a seed-drying facility, with the aim of creating high-value cropping opportunities in the region.

“This new investment builds on that foundation by bringing the full seed value chain together in one location, from drying and cleaning through to processing and storage.

“It reduces the need to transport seed outside the region for processing, meaning growers can retain more value locally while improving efficiency and resilience across the sector.

“The project positions Hawke’s Bay as a key hub for high-value seed production and will help support future growth in the sector."

Central Hawke’s Bay District Council has been working with local seed growers to bring the project to fruition and has coordinated efforts on the RIF application.

The facility will provide processing infrastructure for growers and seed companies across Hawke's Bay and the wider lower North Island, increasing processing capacity outside Canterbury and strengthening domestic supply chains.

The Regional Infrastructure Fund (RIF) funding will be provided as a loan, alongside $750,000 of grower and industry co-funding.

"This investment is about backing Hawke's Bay growers with the infrastructure they need to expand production, increase exports and create long-term opportunities for the region," Mr Patterson says.

news.title: Government backing Whale Trail tourism venture
news.body:
The Government is investing up to $12 million to connect Picton to the Whale Trail cycling and walking track, Transport and Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop and Tourism and Hospitality Minister Louise Upston say.

A proposed bridge over SH1 and the main trunk railway, together with the associated trail works, would provide a direct connection between Picton where many walkers and cyclists disembark the Cook Strait ferries, and the 170km walking and cycling trail along the South Island's northeast coast to Kaikoura.

"The climb out of Picton on SH1 for cyclists has long been acknowledged as a tricky section. They must navigate other ferry traffic which is often heavy, particularly during the holiday periods,” Mr Bishop says.

"The bridge and associated trail work would provide a safer and more direct connection between Picton and the Whale Trail, avoiding this narrow, busy and high-speed section.”

Improving the connection to Picton would complete the Whale Trail, an important step forward for the trail itself and wider tourism across the top of the South Island, Ms Upston says.

"The Whale Trail, already a popular trail with visitors and locals alike, has the potential to attract more visitors to the region, encourage longer stays, and showcase more of what Marlborough and Kaikōura have to offer," Ms Upston says.

"This project is the last part of this tourism infrastructure. Connecting the trail directly to Picton will create a more seamless experience for visitors and strengthen one of New Zealand's premier walking and cycling attractions.”

Mr Bishop says that before any decisions is made on the construction of the bridge, government needs confidence there is a deliverable solution, a clear understanding of costs, and a pathway to successful delivery.

Government support is being provided in stages with up to $1 million from the Regional Infrastructure Fund supporting the New Zealand Transport Agency to undertake bridge investigations, design and planning.

A further $4.4m from the Infrastructure Reference Group Programme will help deliver the final section of the shared walking and cycling trail connection into Picton.

Additional funding of up to $6.6m has been ring-fenced for potential bridge construction, subject to further design work and future decisions.

news.title: Government support for aged care facility
news.body:
A loan from the Regional Infrastructure Fund will help fund a much-needed new 24-bed wing at O’Conor Home for senior citizens in Westport, Regional Development Minister Shane Jones and Associate Health Minister Casey Costello say.

“Providing safe, fit-for-purpose facilities for our senior citizens is a marker of a compassionate and caring society. When older people need this type of specialist care, it should be near their family, friends and community,” Mr Jones says.

The $13.9 million new wing will see capacity at O’Conor Home increase from 68 to 92, providing an additional 10 places for residents requiring dementia care and 14 more hospital-level care beds. Approximately 25 new staff will be recruited to care for the extra residents.

Despite having a much higher proportion of people aged 65 and over than the national average, the West Coast has seen a reduction in specialist aged-care services over the past 10 years, with O’Conor Home the only provider in the Buller district.

“Increasing access to this type of specialist residential care on the West Coast will reduce pressure on the wider health system, particularly hospital services,” Ms Costello says.

“It will also see fewer older people having to go to aged care facilities outside the region. This initiative aligns with our wider aged care reforms which will give people better access to the services they need.”

The O’Conor Institute Trust Board which owns and operates O’Conor Home has also received funding for the project from Health New Zealand, Development West Coast and the wider Buller community.

The RIF loan of $2.1m will ensure the construction-ready project goes ahead as soon as possible, with detailed design and consent work already completed, and it has an anticipated completion date of August 2028.

news.title: Government backing iwi-led geothermal potential
news.body:
Funding for two iwi-led geothermal projects near Rotorua will help build the knowledge needed to better understand the Bay of Plenty’s geothermal potential, Regional Development Minister Shane Jones says.

The Regional Infrastructure Fund will provide a $3.82 million loan towards the $5.53m Ngāti Rangiteaorere geothermal exploration programme in the Tikitere-Ruahine geothermal field, northeast of Rotorua.

A $3m grant will support research into the Waimangu geothermal system, the world’s youngest, formed by the 1886 Mount Tarawera eruption.

“Rotorua has deep geothermal knowledge and capability, and geothermal is already an important part of the Bay of Plenty economy. But there is still much to learn about the region’s geothermal potential and the opportunities it could enable,” Mr Jones says.

“This early-stage work will build that understanding, while supporting Māori land-owner led stewardship and creating opportunities for specialist contractors, skills development and employment during delivery.”

The Ngāti Rangiteaorere geothermal exploration project, led by a subsidiary of the Ngāti Rangiteaorere Koromatua Council, will explore and test the geothermal resource on Ngāti Rangiteaorere land, building a clearer picture of its characteristics and potential future uses.

The Waimangu programme, led by the Ngāti Rangitihi and Tūhourangi Tribal Authority, will undertake research drilling and monitoring to improve understanding of the protected geothermal system, while safeguarding its significant environmental, cultural and tourism va­lues and generating wider public-good knowledge.

“The Government’s From the Ground Up geothermal strategy recognises that high upfront costs, uncertainty and gaps in geothermal knowledge can be barriers to exploration and research. It sets a clear direction for building science and technical capability, strengthening regional economies and supporting iwi and hapū aspirations for geothermal resources,” Mr Jones says.

“These projects put the strategy into action by building knowledge of important geothermal systems, supporting iwi-led stewardship and providing a stronger evidence base for future decisions.”

Any future development leading from the projects would depend on the results of the research and exploration, further funding and investment, regulatory and consenting requirements, and appropriate protection of environmental and cultural values.

RIF grant to help build replacement Tinopai Wharf
news.body:
The dilapidated and closed Tinopai Wharf on Kaipara Harbour will be replaced with the help of a $1 million grant from the Regional Infrastructure Fund, Regional Development Minister Shane Jones says.

“The wharf at Tinopai has been shut because of structural and safety issues for nearly two years. Replacing this important community asset will be good news for local fishers, boaties, and recreational users of the harbour,” Mr Jones says.

The $1.3 million wharf replacement project will initially involve demolition of the run-down wharf, which has damaged and decayed piles beyond repair. The new wharf will be built to closely resemble the existing structure and remain within the same footprint.

“The new wharf will be designed to meet modern marine engineering standards and have improved access for boats. But this is not just a nice-to-have for recreational users and people wanting to catch some kai moana – it can also act as a secondary route in case of an emergency or evacuation in the area.

“Tinopai is vulnerable to isolation because it relies on a single road connection, which has been taken out by weather events in the recent past. When that route is disrupted, there is no alternative land access for residents, emergency services or essential supplies,” Mr Jones says.

The project will be delivered by Kaipara District Council, which was forced to close the facility in late 2023 because of safety concerns. The new wharf is expected to be operational in 2028, subject to design work being completed and appropriate consents secured.

Along with recreational benefits, the new wharf will offer opportunities for future economic growth in the area such as tourism and fishing ventures on the unique Kaipara Harbour.

news.title: Government support for Turner Centre upgrade
news.body:
A Regional Infrastructure Fund grant will be used to modernise Kerikeri’s Turner Centre, helping the Far North town play host to more cultural, community and business events, Regional Development Minister Shane Jones says.

The grant of up to $3 million will go towards the first stage of a $6.3 million upgrade of the centre’s Plaza and Event Centre.

“This Regional Infrastructure Fund grant will help a remarkable community-built and supported venue take its offering to the next level,” Mr Jones says.

“Some 20 years ago, the Kerikeri community had the vision and determination to raise more than $12 million to build the Turner Centre, and it has punched well above its weight ever since.

“It has hosted major productions, conferences and community events that might otherwise have bypassed Tai Tokerau, including performances by the New Zealand Symphony Orchestra and Royal New Zealand Ballet.”

The first stage of the upgrade will include better ventilation and acoustics, new audio-visual and technical systems, and improved accessibility and amenities, cultural design elements, furniture and finishes.

The work will improve the venue’s functionality and allow different parts of the centre to be used at the same time, opening the door to more commercial and community activity.

“The Turner Centre is far more than a theatre venue as it has different spaces to welcome community classes, exhibitions, kapa haka, and major touring performances.

“These events generate valuable economic activity by attracting people into the town from across Northland and further away, supporting local accommodation, hospitality and other businesses.”

The project’s commencement is subject to completion of detailed design, consenting, procurement and other pre-construction requirements being met. The project is expected to be completed by the end of 2027.

news.title: Year 11 Agriculture and Horticultural Science subject announced
news.body:
Students will be able to study Agriculture and Horticultural Science from Year 11, creating a clear pathway into Years 12 and 13 and future careers in New Zealand's primary industries, Education Minister Erica Stanford says.

“Year 11 Agriculture and Horticultural Science will be an optional subject alongside compulsory Science, giving students the opportunity to develop specialist knowledge and pursue their interests earlier.

“It complements the existing Agriculture and Horticultural Science subjects at Years 12 and 13, as well as the new industry-led Food and Fibre subject currently being developed for Years 12 and 13, giving students a wide range of pathways into New Zealand's primary industries.

“The Ministry of Education's original intention was that schools could teach Year 11 Science through an agriculture and horticulture lens, providing a pathway into more specialised science subjects in Years 12 and 13.

“However, since the release of the new Year 11 Science curriculum, feedback from rural school principals, teachers and the primary sector has made it clear that this approach could not provide the flexibility originally envisaged, and that Agriculture and Horticultural Science would be better delivered as a standalone subject.

“We've listened to that feedback and are making Agriculture and Horticultural Science a standalone subject from Year 11.

“New Zealand's primary industries are the backbone of our economy and a major driver of our exports. We want more young people to see the opportunities available in these industries and develop the knowledge and skills they need to pursue rewarding, high-paying careers.”

The Ministry of Education will work with subject matter experts to develop the new Year 11 subject, alongside teaching and assessment resources and implementation support for schools and teachers.

Schools will have the flexibility to decide whether to offer the subject, allowing them to respond to the needs and interests of their students and communities.

Public consultation on the new Year 11 subject is expected to begin in the coming weeks.

“This is about backing our rural communities, strengthening pathways into our primary industries, and making sure our education system prepares young New Zealanders for the opportunities ahead.”

news.title: Rockpool pillagers face infringements soon
news.body:
People who break new rules aimed at protecting rockpools in and around Auckland and Coromandel will face infringement fees from this month, Oceans and Fisheries Minister Shane Jones says.

“Last month I announced new protections for Auckland and Coromandel rockpools and intertidal areas to address overharvesting and help restore these important coastal habitats.”

“From November 26, Fishery Officers will be armed with a new tool – the ability to issue infringement notices, which carry a $250 penalty.

“The new infringement regime gives Fishery Officers an option that sits between the current options of education of rule-breakers, and court action.

“People who take more than they should, or take species protected under the rules of the closure, are on notice that they will feel it in their hip pockets,” Mr Jones says.

More serious offenders will still face prosecution and risk having anything in the commission of the offence seized, including vehicles.

“Kiwis told us clearly during consultation that stronger protections had to be backed by effective enforcement, and these changes will help ensure the rules are complied with.”

The intertidal closure came into force on 1 November and will help stop the overharvesting of coastal shellfish and marine life across the Auckland and Coromandel coastlines.

To support the new rules, Fisheries New Zealand is placing signs in the relevant areas, educating people about the changes, and running an extensive six-week awareness campaign.

Full details on the new restrictions can be found on MPI’s website.

news.title: Green light for Rotorua business park intersection
news.body:
A $3.46 million grant from the Regional Infrastructure Fund will provide safer access to Rotorua’s Eastgate Business Park from State Highway 30, Regional Development Minister Shane Jones and Transport Minister Chris Bishop say.

A four-way intersection controlled by traffic lights at the junction of SH30 and Wahanga-A-Rangi Crescent will improve safety on the busy highway, support development at the business park and provide for future access to the planned Rotorua Airport Business Park nearby.

“Having safe, suitable access to Eastgate will support development at the site and future-proof the wider area for more growth,” Mr Jones says.

“This investment reflects the Regional Infrastructure Fund’s focus on backing practical regional infrastructure that unlocks economic opportunities.”

Mr Bishop says building one road intersection to serve both business parks is the most practical approach.

“It will serve existing businesses while providing for the airport business park as it develops,” Mr Bishop says.

“Creating future-proofed transport links now means less work as the area gets busier with industry and more vehicle movements.”

The project will be managed by Rotorua Lakes Council. Construction is expected to begin in the next few months, subject to final confirmation and contractors being secured.

news.title: RIF grant to support energy resilience in Far North
news.body:
A grant of $1.11 million from the Regional Infrastructure Fund will support a Māori-led initiative to install solar power, battery storage and back-up generators in community facilities in the Far North, Regional Development Minister Shane Jones and Māori Development Minister Tama Potaka say.

Mr Jones says the investment will strengthen local energy resilience and help maintain essential services in some of Northland’s remote communities when power is disrupted.

“This is what energy resilience looks like in practical terms – trusted local facilities supporting their communities when severe weather cuts power and closes roads.”

“Tai Tokerau gets more than its fair share of severe weather, and our remote communities need the right equipment that can support them until help arrives.

“This investment will harness renewable energy for everyday use while helping keep the lights on, water flowing and communications open when conditions are at their worst.”

The funding to deliver the programme will go to Tū Mai Rā Energy, an iwi-owned renewable energy company with experience installing solar systems for marae and remote communities.

Mr Potaka says marae are community anchors, particularly in remote areas.

“Marae play a critical role for whānau and the wider population when hardship or emergencies strike. Equipping them and other community facilities with renewable and back-up power will help them meet everyday energy needs and continue support when normal services are disrupted.”

news.title: Christchurch commuter rail pilot to be funded
news.body:
The Regional Infrastructure Fund will invest in supporting Mainland Rail to return passenger rail services to Christchurch for a 12-month trial and establish the Christchurch-Dunedin-Invercargill Mainlander as a regular service, Rail Minister Winston Peters and Regional Development Minister Shane Jones say.

“New Zealand’s railways began in Christchurch in 1863, and it is time we put them back to use again for passenger rail, not just freight and tourism,” Mr Peters says.

Mainland Rail, which owns rail carriages, intends to provide a 12-month trial service to test Canterbury’s appetite for rail as a public transport service and run more frequent trains from Christchurch-Dunedin-Invercargill. The Regional Infrastructure Fund (RIF) will provide a loan of $3.4 million to support these initiatives.

The trains will run morning and evening commuter services on the main lines from Rangiora in the north and Rolleston in the south into central Christchurch starting in mid-2027. The Rolleston trip is expected to take less than 20 minutes by rail instead of 50 minutes by road, taking commuter traffic off are already busy roads.

“New Zealanders are sick of transport proposals costing hundreds of millions or billions when pragmatic solutions such as using what we already have are staring us in the face, as is the case in Christchurch and its rail system,” Mr Peters says.

“The fares will be announced closer to the start date, but we are talking about a public transport trial and would expect affordable fares similar to those paid by rail commuters in Wellington and Auckland.

“There’s a saying, ‘it works in practice but will it work in theory,’ and here is an opportunity for Cantabrians to prove their support for rail as public transport in practice.

“The service proceeding is subject to the local councils confirming their combined half of costs, and letters of support from the Mayors of Christchurch, Selwyn and Waimakariri, and we look forward to engaging further with Environment Canterbury,” Mr Peters says.

The $3.4 million RIF funding will also support Mainland Rail to shift its Mainlander train from monthly excursions to a regular timetable between Christchurch, Ashburton, Timaru, Oamaru, Dunedin, Gore and Invercargill.

“The South Island’s rail corridors are regional infrastructure assets, and this funding is about putting them back to work for communities, tourism and local economies,” Mr Jones says.

“This is the type of commonsense investment people want to see – using what we already have, reinstating what we once had, and giving people choices in their lives once again.

“The economic development benefits are obvious: railing people into Canterbury, Otago and Southland towns to spend in the local economies, strengthening tourism in the South Island, creating employment, and putting assets New Zealanders already own to better use for the benefit of our economy,” Mr Jones says.

Mainland Rail will now start necessary planning processes with councils, the rail regulator, and KiwiRail – with start dates to be announced by Mainland Rail closer to the time.

“We look forward to the restored Mataura Railway Station reopening in late 2027 thanks to our commitment to fund its restoration in 2025, and we are confident the Mainlander will return to Mataura then too,” Mr Peters says.

news.title: Work begins on Warkworth to Te Hana motorway
news.body:
Breaking ground on one of New Zealand's most important transport infrastructure projects – Warkworth to Te Hana – marks a significant step towards greater economic growth for Auckland, Northland and the upper North Island, Transport Minister Chris Bishop says.

Mr Bishop joined project partners, mana whenua and stakeholders today to turn the first sod on the Warkworth to Te Hana section of the Northland Expressway, kicking off construction on the first Road of National Significance in the wider Northland Corridor.

"The Warkworth to Te Hana motorway will create a safer, more resilient and more reliable connection between Auckland and Northland, improving freight efficiency and making journeys easier for the thousands of people who use this corridor every day.

"The motorway is expected to prevent 145 deaths and serious injuries over its lifetime, save motorists between seven and ten minutes per journey, and take around 1,000 heavy vehicles a day off the existing SH1 route through Wellsford and Te Hana."

The motorway will connect directly to the 18-kilometre Pūhoi to Warkworth motorway, which opened in 2023, via a free-flow interchange at Woodcocks Road, providing an alternative to the existing State Highway 1 (SH1) route through the Dome Valley.

The new route will begin west of Warkworth, pass east of Wellsford and Te Hana, and reconnect with SH1 near Waimanu Road. It will feature 15 bridges, two underpasses, numerous large culverts, 12 wetland stormwater treatment basins and twin tunnels through Kraack Hill above Dome Valley.

"Northland's economic success depends on reliable transport links. This investment will help unlock growth opportunities, improve productivity and give businesses greater confidence that people and goods can move efficiently between Northland and Auckland," Mr Bishop says.

"The project is expected to cost $3.65 billion in Net Present Value terms, covering NZTA management costs, design and construction, financing, maintenance and operations. It has a positive Benefit Cost Ratio of 1.6, including wider economic benefits, meaning the economic benefits are expected to outweigh the costs."

Delivered through a Public Private Partnership, the project will be designed, built, financed, operated and maintained by the Northway consortium, alongside New Zealand partners including Downer New Zealand and AECOM.

"The construction of this motorway will also provide a significant boost to the local economy, with around 60 per cent of physical works expenditure expected to flow through local supply chains.

"The project will support around 400 site-based roles, growing to approximately 1,000 people during main construction.

"Northway has also committed to supporting workforce development through internships, apprenticeships, graduate roles and school-to-work pathways, with a particular focus on opportunities for local communities, Māori and Pasifika."

Initial work will focus on detailed design, site preparation and enabling works before major construction activity ramps up next year. The motorway is expected to open to traffic in 2033.

"This project delivers on the Government's commitment to build the infrastructure New Zealand needs. Today's sod turning demonstrates progress on a motorway that will provide lasting benefits for generations to come," Mr Bishop says.

Notes for editors:

The Northway consortium comprises Acciona Concesiones SL, Aberdeen Investments, Global Sustainable Infrastructure GP IV Ltd and Acciona Construction New Zealand Ltd. The Project Agreement between the Crown and the Northway consortium was signed in July 2026.

news.title: Gisborne’s flood protection strengthened
news.body:
Gisborne City and 10,000ha of some of the region’s most productive land are now better protected from flooding, following the completion of the Waipaoa Flood Control Scheme, Regional Development Minister Shane Jones says.

“The people of Tairāwhiti can feel proud of what has been achieved here. Since 2019, approximately 64km of stopbanks along both sides of Waipaoa River have been widened and raised, providing a higher level of protection designed to withstand a one-in-100-year flood event,” Mr Jones says.

“In key locations, stopbanks have been widened to up to 4m and raised by as much as 2m to protect communities and valuable food-producing land.

“Cyclone Gabrielle demonstrated the importance of this work and the need to finish the job. Even before the project was fully completed, upgraded sections of the scheme provided greater protection for around 7000ha of residential and horticultural land,” Mr Jones says.

Mr Jones attended an event at Waipaoa River today to officially mark the completion of the scheme.

Crown support for the scheme included a $7.5 million grant through the COVID-19 Response and Recovery Fund in 2020 and a further $18.4m through the Cyclone Recovery Programme in 2023.

“These investments accelerated Gisborne District Council’s work, bringing the scheme’s completion forward by four years. The completed scheme will strengthen the region's resilience for decades to come, helping safeguard homes, transport links, public infrastructure, and the horticultural, viticultural and farming land that underpins the Tairāwhiti economy.”

The total cost of the project was $35.1m and included $9.2m in co-funding from Gisborne District Council.

news.body: In order to perform its statutory tasks, the SNB provides the financial system with central bank liquidity against sufficient collateral. The SNB's collateral policy protects its balance sheet and ensures that liquidity is provided in an effective, efficient and transparent manner. The SNB GC Basket plays a key role in the implementation of monetary policy and in supporting payments. It combines high quality requirements with a broad, international focus, and has also become established as the collateral standard in the Swiss interbank repo market. This common standard and the integrated market infrastructure facilitate the mobilisation of collateral, thereby supporting the effective implementation of monetary policy and the smooth functioning of payments. The SNB reviews its collateral policy on an ongoing basis and adjusts it as necessary to take account of changed market conditions and technological developments.

news.title: RIF funds new Gisborne medical research centre
news.body:
A new building at Mātai Medical Research Institute will expand medical research, specialist healthcare and education opportunities in Tairāwhiti, supported by a $20 million loan from the Regional Infrastructure Fund, Regional Development Minister Shane Jones says.

“In its short history, Mātai has put Tairāwhiti on the map with what it has achieved in advanced medical imaging and neuroscience research. They are true pioneers in translating preventative and predictive healthcare research into real-world health solutions,” Mr Jones says.

“This RIF investment will give Mātai the opportunity to bring more research, technology and health-related activity into Gisborne, and create opportunities for Tairāwhiti people to develop the skills needed to take part in that growth.”

Mr Jones announced the funding from the Regional Infrastructure Fund (RIF) at a visit to Mātai today.

The $28.4 million project involves the construction and fit-out of a new three-storey Mātai Innovation Centre adjacent to the Institute’s existing Mātai Imaging Research Centre building. It will include primary healthcare research facilities, specialist clinics, a day procedure unit, education spaces, and supporting infrastructure and parking.

Once the new building is operational, it is expected Mātai will support more than 150 full- and part-time roles. It will also increase the Tairāwhiti region’s access to advanced medical research, diagnostic services and specialist healthcare services currently only available in larger centres.

The ongoing development at Mātai continues to strengthen Tairāwhiti’s health science and innovation ecosystem, helping the region build a more diverse economy based on knowledge and innovation. Education and research placements at the centre are projected to double to more than 100 a year by 2035.

“Mātai is creating pathways into education, research and high-skilled employment that would typically only be available in our big cities or overseas. It shows that cutting-edge research and innovation do not need to be concentrated in our biggest cities – our regions can and should be the drivers of innovation,” Mr Jones says.

Construction of the new building will create approximately 70 jobs and is expected to be completed by April 2029, dependent on design milestones and consents being secured. Mātai is working closely with Trust Tairāwhiti and Gisborne Holdings Limited, the commercial arm of Gisborne District Council, as regional partners on the project.

news.title: Opening of new Tongan detector dog facility
news.body:
Customs Minister Casey Costello is travelling to Tonga this evening to represent New Zealand at the official opening of the country’s second detector dog facility.

“The new facility in Vava’u will help strengthen Tonga’s border and build local capability to combat organised crime and the drug trade,” Ms Costello says.

“Transnational, serious and organised crime (TSOC) is a growing challenge across the Pacific with criminal networks exploiting legitimate trade and travel to move illicit drugs, firearms and cash across borders.

“New Zealand is committed to working with our Pacific neighbours to address this and the facility is a practical investment in Tonga’s security and that of the region.”

New Zealand Customs and New Zealand Police worked alongside Tonga Police and Tonga’s Ministry of Revenue and Customs to deliver the project, with the facility being built locally.

Vava’u has an international airport, and its port and regular yacht and small-craft traffic create an environment where strong border capability is important. The facility, located within the Tonga Police compound in Neiafu, will give Tonga’s detector dog teams a secure base on the island and will provide greater capability to screen passengers, baggage, cargo and maritime activity, and allow teams to deploy for longer periods in support of operations. The facility will be jointly owned by Tonga Police and Tonga Customs.

“We want to work alongside Pacific partners in a way that supports their priorities and builds sustainable, locally led capability,” Ms Costello says. “The Pacific Detector Dog Programme is a great example of that approach, and the opening of this new facility represents another step in the partnership between our two nations.”

In Tonga, three qualified detector dog teams are already operating out of Nuku’alofa, with two further teams - one Tonga Police team and one Tonga Customs team - currently training at the New Zealand Police Dog Training Centre in Trentham. These teams will provide the workforce required to support operations from the new Vava’u facility.

The opening event is occurring Friday morning and will be attended by Tongan Deputy Prime Minister Dr Viliami Uasike Latu, the Minister of Revenue and Customs Hon Sevenitini Toumo’ua and the Governor of Vava’u, Lord Fakatulolo.

Minister Costello will return to New Zealand tomorrow night.

news.title: Northland to get fourth Rural Training Hub
news.body:
Northland will soon have a Rural Training Hub to help grow the rural health workforce and improve access to healthcare for communities across the region, Associate Health Minister Matt Doocey announced today.

“One in five New Zealanders live in rural communities, and they should not be disadvantaged when it comes to accessing timely, quality healthcare,” Mr Doocey says.

“The Government is focused on fixing the basics and building the future by training more health professionals closer to the communities they will serve.

“Rural communities know that when you train people locally, they’re far more likely to stay local. That’s exactly what these hubs are designed to do.”

The Northland hub is the fourth Rural Training Hub to be rolled out nationally, following South Taranaki, Wairoa and the West Coast, which was announced earlier this year.

The hub will support education and training across primary, community and hospital services, helping to build a rural health workforce that reflects the needs of local communities.

“It will support students into clinical placements, create stronger training pathways and provide pastoral support to help attract and retain frontline health workers across Northland.

“We know communities understand what works best for them. That’s why the hub will better align workforce planning with communities’ needs.

“It will also give more people exposure to rural health careers and strengthen the pathway between undergraduate and postgraduate rural training.

“This is a practical step towards strengthening rural health services and ensuring communities across New Zealand can access the care they need, closer to home.”

news.title: Lower Hutt gets Crisis Recovery Café
news.body:
Those in need of mental health or addiction support will have another place to go with a new Crisis Recovery Café officially opening today in Lower Hutt, Mental Health Minister Matt Doocey says.

“The new Café, Te Kāhua Ora, will provide a safe, welcoming place where people can talk to someone who understands what they are going through and get the support they need,” Mr Doocey says.

“We know a busy ED is not always the best environment for someone experiencing mental distress. The new café will give people another place to go, without needing a referral, where they can access support from people with their own lived experience, including advocacy and help connecting with other services if needed.”

“That’s why we are rolling out Crisis Recovery Cafés across the country, giving people more options to get support closer to home.

“There is real power in having someone in the room who has their own lived experience and understands what it is like, and the rollout of more peer-led support like this has proved to be a real gamechanger for people.

“Each community is different, which is why I have always said some of the best solutions already exist within our grassroots organisations, they just need to be backed.

“Te Paepae Ārahi Trust has more than 30 years’ experience supporting people across the Hutt Valley and wider Wellington region and will work alongside Kites Trust to deliver the new café.

“Kites Trust already delivers the peer support service in Wellington Hospital’s emergency department, helping support people who do need to present to an ED.

“Together, these organisations bring valuable lived experience and local knowledge to help ensure people in Lower Hutt can access the support that works for them.”

The café will open on Friday 30 October and will initially operate from 3pm to 9pm, Wednesday to Saturday. Opening hours will get reviewed to ensure they are meeting community needs.

“Peer support specialists will also be introduced in Hutt Hospital’s emergency department, with the service expected to be operating by early 2027.

“We are continuing to build a better future by delivering faster access to support, more frontline workers and a better crisis response.”

news.title: New Vanguard charter school to offer military-ethos education to Kiwi students
news.body:
Associate Education Minister David Seymour has today announced that Vanguard Prep School will open on the North Shore, Auckland in Term 1 next year, offering a new option for students in Years 7 to 10.

“Every child deserves the chance to learn and grow in ways which are more specific to their needs. Vanguard Prep School will give more students that opportunity,” Mr Seymour says.

"The team behind Vanguard Military School has shown they can connect with young people and help them succeed. They ran a successful charter school under the previous charter school programme. Despite this, Labour shut the charter school programme down.

“This new school is about bringing those strengths to younger students at a stage when good habits and self-belief can make a real difference.

“With a focus on discipline, leadership and academic achievement, Vanguard Prep School aims to help young people succeed at school and build strong foundations for their future.

“Drawing on the military ethos that underpins Vanguard's approach, students, known as recruits, will begin their day with a morning parade before moving into small academic classes focused on literacy, numeracy and core subjects.

"Afternoons will include physical training, team challenges and activities designed to develop teamwork, leadership and self-discipline.

“Every student will belong to a small section of around 20 students led by a dedicated teacher who works closely with both students and parents.

“While the school has a connection to Vanguard Military School, students attending Vanguard Prep will be set up with the skills they need to succeed at any secondary school they move on to.

“There are more ideas in the communities of New Zealand than there are in the Government. That’s why we open ideas to the wider community and apply strict

performance standards to the best ones.

“The charter school equation is: the same funding as state schools, plus greater flexibility plus stricter accountability for results, equals student success.

"Vanguard Prep School will provide another path for students and families seeking an education built around structure, high expectations, and academic excellence, and I look forward to seeing it open its doors next year.”
